items.title: Speculative Decoding in Production
items.abstract:
Speculative Decoding in Production was recorded as a Lightning Talk session at the 2026 AI Engineering Summit. The session focuses on serving and optimizing large models under real production constraints. The project referenced by this session is ggml-org/llama.cpp. Programme notes describe the project as: the open-source llama.cpp project, which the speaker uses as the reference implementation for the techniques shown on stage. The speaker combines architecture diagrams, production anecdotes, and benchmark results, and reserves time at the end for questions from practitioners.

The speaker frames serving as a scheduling problem: requests, KV cache blocks, batching windows, and hardware memory all compete for the same resources.

Quantization is presented as a pipeline rather than a single switch: calibration, outlier handling, kernel support, and accuracy regression checks all matter.

The speaker highlights easy wins first: better batching, fewer copies, tighter tokenizers, and honest load tests before investing in exotic kernels.

A final segment maps model size and context length to realistic single-node and multi-node deployment envelopes.

Continuous batching and paged attention are explained through production traces rather than benchmark charts, including the tail latency effects that appear when long and short requests mix.

A detailed section covers cache reuse, prefix sharing, and eviction policies, with guidance on when the complexity of a shared cache pays for itself.

Method and measurement. A cost table compares tokens, latency, engineering hours, and operational risk for each option discussed. Failure analysis is given as much time as the success story, including a list of assumptions that did not survive contact with real traffic. The team used a staged rollout with canary traffic, automatic rollback, and a weekly review of quality regressions. The session includes a short live debugging segment in which a deliberately broken configuration is diagnosed from traces.

Takeaways. A second takeaway is that observability and evaluation must be designed together with the feature. Attendees should leave with a concrete checklist for reproducing the core result in their own environment. The session ends with a short reading list and an invitation to contribute issues and reproduction scripts to the referenced project. The speaker recommends starting with the simplest configuration that satisfies the product requirement.

Session context. The speaker contrasted research prototypes with systems that must run unattended overnight and recover from partial failures. The speaker used production incidents as teaching material and was candid about what failed before the final design. The room was full, and the questions after the talk focused on deployment details rather than demos.

The speaker drew a distinction between a demo that succeeds once and a system that succeeds repeatedly under noisy inputs.

The speaker answered a question about security by describing the permission model, the sandbox boundary, and the review process for sensitive actions.

Audience questions ranged from hardware selection to team structure, and the answers consistently returned to clarity of measurement.

The talk included a short retrospective on what the team would do differently if they started again with the same constraints.

A comparison slide showed the same workload before and after the change, with percentile latencies rather than averages so that tail behavior was visible.

Several recommendations were framed as defaults that teams can start with and then relax only after measuring the tradeoff in their own environment.

A follow-up workshop covers the hands-on version of the same material, with exercises that rebuild a small end-to-end pipeline.

The session included a brief discussion of privacy, including how long traces are retained and how user data is scrubbed before storage.

The presentation closed with an open invitation to reproduce the benchmark and report divergence, since negative results are also useful.

During the audience discussion, one participant described a similar rollout that stalled because ownership was split across teams; the speaker recommended a single service owner for the end-to-end workflow.

The presenter emphasized that tooling should make the safe path the easy path, because operators under pressure tend to take shortcuts.

items.abstract:
A Tour of the Reference Model Context Protocol Servers was recorded as a Workshop session at the 2026 AI Engineering Summit. The session focuses on the engineering of reliable agents, tool use, orchestration, and state management. The project referenced by this session is modelcontextprotocol/servers. Programme notes describe the project as: A collection of reference server implementations that expose tools, resources, and prompts to agents through the Model Context Protocol. The speaker combines architecture diagrams, production anecdotes, and benchmark results, and reserves time at the end for questions from practitioners.

Several examples show how to keep an agent grounded in an environment: sandboxed file systems, browser sessions, shell access, and structured observations that the model can verify.

The speaker opens with a taxonomy of agent runtimes: planners, executors, tool routers, memory services, and policy layers that decide when an autonomous loop should stop and ask for help.

A recurring theme is that tool interfaces are the real contract. Schemas drift, permissions change, and retries multiply unless every tool call is validated, traced, and bounded by an explicit timeout.

The talk closes with cost and latency accounting, showing where orchestration overhead dominates and how caching, batching, and concurrency limits change the economics of agent products.

The session compares single-agent loops with multi-agent topologies and argues that most production failures come from unclear handoffs rather than weak models.

Observability receives a full section. The speaker demonstrates span-level traces that connect a user request to each planning step, tool invocation, retry, and final artifact.

items.title: Open Datasets for Instruction Tuning
items.abstract:
Open Datasets for Instruction Tuning was recorded as a Workshop session at the 2026 AI Engineering Summit. The session focuses on training recipes, adapters, and data-centric model improvement. The project referenced by this session is huggingface/datasets. The speaker combines architecture diagrams, production anecdotes, and benchmark results, and reserves time at the end for questions from practitioners.

Regularization, replay data, and curriculum design are presented as tools for preserving general capability while specializing behavior.

The session covers distributed training failure modes: stragglers, checkpoint storms, network contention, and silent numerical issues.

A case study walks through a failed fine-tune, the diagnostics that exposed the problem, and the data changes that recovered model quality.

Parameter-efficient methods are compared on memory, throughput, and the effort required to merge and serve adapters in production.

Evaluation during training is framed as a budget allocation problem, with guidance on when to run full suites and when fast proxies are enough.

The speaker explains how to choose sequence length, packing strategy, and gradient accumulation so that the effective batch size matches the recipe.

The session includes a short live debugging segment in which a deliberately broken configuration is diagnosed from traces. Each experiment reports hardware, batch sizes, prompt templates, and evaluation settings so the audience can judge how far the result will transfer. items.title: Evaluating Long-Context Benchmarks
items.abstract:
Evaluating Long-Context Benchmarks was recorded as a Main Track session at the 2026 AI Engineering Summit. The session focuses on measurement, benchmarking, red-teaming, and guardrails for deployed models. The project referenced by this session is EleutherAI/lm-evaluation-harness. The speaker combines architecture diagrams, production anecdotes, and benchmark results, and reserves time at the end for questions from practitioners.

Red-teaming is presented as a continuous program with ownership, triage, and regression tests rather than a one-off exercise.

The session distinguishes offline quality checks, online guardrails, and incident review, showing how each catches different failures.

Safety filters are evaluated on both false positives and false negatives, because over-blocking quietly destroys user trust and product metrics.

The speaker starts from the observation that evaluation is a product requirement, not a research afterthought, and that ambiguous metrics create false confidence.

The talk examines contamination, leakage, and benchmark saturation, with practical tests for detecting them before leaders rely on a score.

Benchmark construction is described step by step: task sampling, rubric design, annotator agreement, and adversarial case mining.
